contentHtml:
Sabarinath Nair, CEO and Founder, Skillveri, discusses how the company is applying its industrial skills training expertise to VR-led stroke rehabilitation, with a focus on patient-centric design, remote recovery monitoring and the role of clinicians in treatment decisions, in an interview with Neha Aathavale

What made you identify healthcare, and specifically post-stroke rehabilitation, as the right market for you to enter? Beyond the obvious unmet need, what did you see in the healthcare ecosystem or patient journey that made you believe this was an area where your technology could create meaningful value? 

Skillveri has been building solutions for high precision industrial skills training for the past 14 years. Every activity or task that a human performs in everyday life is essentially a skill which the brain has learnt over time, even though it may be so small or so natural that we don’t think of it as a skill. A person affected by stroke is unable to use their limbs because the brain loses a part of it which knows how to do these activities. 

When we realised that stroke rehab is basically retraining other parts of the brain to relearn the skills it has lost, we felt this would be a very meaningful application for Skillveri’s core strength of skill training. Using technology to deliver therapy will make it more engaging for the users and hence lesser chances of discontinuing. It also addresses the current limitations of availability of devices and trained therapists, and makes it possible to use therapist time more efficiently. It will also make a lot of difference as the recovery process becomes completely measurable, with clinicians and therapists being able to monitor progress continuously 

Skillveri has spent years building immersive training technologies for automotive and manufacturing. What did you have to fundamentally rethink when applying that expertise to rehabilitation, where patient safety, clinical outcomes and clinician acceptance are as important as the technology itself? How did your collaboration with SCTIMST influence those decisions? 

The key thing to remember when building such a product is user empathy. While our training for industries focus on what the user ‘must do’, in a context like rehab it completely changes to what the user ‘can do’. The system has to adapt to the user, instead of the user meeting the system’s requirements. You have to keep in mind the limitations of the person using it, design it in such a way that it does not feel overwhelming, the user feels motivated to keep using it, yet meets all the clinical requirements. 

The team at SCTIMST helped with structuring it systematically – which joints to be focused on, which positions need what kind of movements, the sequence in which they should be built, etc. We brought in Skillveri’s expertise in technology & gamification and converted those into user friendly modules. 

XTend uses markerless tracking through the VR headset camera, without wearable sensors or wires. What specific limitation of existing rehabilitation technology were you trying to overcome with this approach? And as you move from controlled clinical environments to patients using the system at home, how do you balance ease of use with the level of accuracy required for meaningful clinical monitoring? 

Keeping the entire system minimalistic, to just one single wireless VR headset, eliminates complex equipment and provides comfort and ease of use to patients. It can be carried easily anywhere, making it possible for therapists to take it to multiple patients’ homes and deploy it under their supervision, instead of the patients needing to visit a clinic for continued therapy.

The exercises are scientifically precise and have been designed based on continuous therapist inputs, so that the efficacy of the therapy remains at par or better with the clinical levels required at each step. The system is also meant to be used initially under the supervision of a therapist only, until the patient is ready enough for independent use. 

XTend uses AI to adapt exercise difficulty and cloudbased monitoring to track recovery remotely. Where do you see technology genuinely improving rehabilitation, and where do you think human clinical judgement will remain indispensable? How are you defining that boundary as the product evolves? 

We see technology as an aid for efficacy. The data will make it easier for the clinician to monitor progress over time, and make focused and individualised treatment choices, but it will be their experience and expertise that will decide the course of actions based on the data. Having more meaningful and actionable data equips clinicians to make the decisions that will result in the best possible patient outcomes. That judgement will be indispensable as they place the assistive technology within a wider context of various other factors unique to each patient. 

What is the business model you see emerging for VR-led rehabilitation in India, and what will need to change across hospitals, clinicians, patients and reimbursement for a solution like XTend to scale beyond individual institutions? 

The most viable model we think currently would be for hospitals and therapy centres to adopt the units and deploy it through their therapists, while we are also looking at the potential in the future for solutions that are more accessible to individual users themselves. The key thing needed for scale is to create awareness on the potential and possibilities of using technology like VR for stroke recovery, and look at it as a mainstream therapy solution instead of a niche option.
